newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-WHSmith under pressure as CEO quits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-WHSmith under pressure as CEO quits.

text.p: W.H. Smith Group Plc's shares fell steeply on Monday after the British retailing group announced chief executive Bill Cockburn was quitting to join British Telecom.

Smith, which posted its first loss in more than 200 years last summer, saw its shares drop nearly eight percent after the surprise news of Cockburn's departure. They stood 31.5 pence lower at 380 pence by midmorning.
Cockburn, who joined Smith just eighteen months ago, will be leaving the group in the middle of a vital campaign to revitalise its core chain.

The stores, on nearly every "high street" around the country, have been struggling to combat increasingly cut-throat competition from margin-hungry food superstores such as ASDA Group Plc and Tesco Plc, which have muscled in on its traditional market for newspapers, books and videos.

Cockburn was brought in in November 1995 to shake up the retailer and find a way to secure the future of the W.H.Smith chain. His departure inevitably increased uncertainty about Smith's prospects, analysts said.
"The shares have fallen because people saw Cockburn as the saviour for Smith, but his move to BT is quite understandable," said one analyst.

Chairman Jeremy Hardie said that Cockburn had been a catalyst for change within the group, presiding over the sale of several of Smith's non-core businesses, notably Do It All home improvement stores and Business Supplies.
Cockburn said in the statement, "Normally I would have wanted to see my plans through to fruition. My decision to join BT was not taken lightly but it is the chance of a lifetime for me."
Hardie told Reuters in a telephone interview the chief executive's departure had nothing to do with problems at the retailing group.
He said Cockburn, who will leave Smith's in October, had received an "irresistible" offer from BT and his decision to leave did not reflect any difficulties at W.H.Smith.
"It's not to do with any problems, it's to do with an irresistible offer," Hardie said.
Cockburn also told Reuters the decision to leave was "all to do with this glittering opportunity at BT and mustn't be interpreted that there are problems here."
Cockburn said BT had approached him and offered the job of managing director of BT in the UK, which was too good an offer to turn down.

Cockburn said he would be running BT in the UK after the company completes its merger with U.S. telecoms group MCI Communications Corp. He said there was a certain irony in the BT job as he had started his working life at the company.
He said W.H. Smith's new management team, including Beverley Hodson, the newly appointed managing director of the core retail chain, were well placed to drive the business forward.
The company made a profit in the first half, but retail analysts are still worried about the long term future of the core W.H. Smith chain.

The UK food retailers' search for higher margins by selling more non-food goods has eaten away at W.H. Smith's traditional market, and analysts said Cockburn faced a tough job trying to reverse this trend.

Cockburn acknowledged there was more to do in terms of the high street chain, but insisted it had tremendous strengths. "It's a very strong brand, it's going to be around for a very long time," he said.
Hardie said the group was already looking for a replacement for Cockburn, but declined to speculate on how long it might take.
There had been speculation in the British press about management discontent after the departure of Smith's commercial director Brent Wilkinson earlier this month.
Cockburn dismissed the speculation saying the senior management team running W.H.Smith retail were "absolutely united in implementing the strategy for success."
He said Hodson had decided to focus more closely on the commercial side of the business and she had a very clear programme of action.
W.H.Smith also said its results for the year to March 31, 1997 would be within the range of market expectations.
The retailer said sales in the second half were up six percent overall and ahead three percent on a comparable store basis.
